extracted.intended_audience: media studies students, researchers, and journalists studying popular/tabloid journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze the rhetorical conventions and newsworthiness criteria British tabloids use to construct a community identity, and contrast those values with broadsheet norms. Useful for evaluating tabloid content, headlines, and editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-establishment slang
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic register signaling skepticism of elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informal, anti-authority vocabulary to position the paper with ordinary readers and distance it from elite institutions; contrasts with broadsheet formality. Anti-pattern: overly technical or deferential language that undermines populist stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiar first names
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling subjects by first names (vs. broadsheet 'Mr./Mrs./surname').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-name usage creates intimacy and familiarity with subjects, reducing social distance; signals membership in the imagined community. Avoid formal honorifics that create distance from readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric of violent encounter
rubrics_metrics.description: Depicting events as battles, clashes, or violent encounters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame events as dramatic physical or moral fights to heighten emotional engagement and simplify complexity into conflict narratives. Examples: fight/battle metaphors for political or social disputes. Anti-pattern: neutral, analytical framing that downplays conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary good vs. evil framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists, juxtapositions, and moral polarities that present issues in black-and-white terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify stories into clear moral oppositions to facilitate reader allegiance and judgment; use juxtapositions and moralizing language. Avoid nuanced or ambivalent presentations that complicate clear moral winners/losers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-page headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual dominance created by headlines that run across pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bold, cross-page, attention-grabbing headlines and layout techniques to assert visual primacy and create spectacle. Guidance relates to page design and headline placement as rhetorical tools, not just copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salacious storylines
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on sex, scandal, and transgression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize stories with erotic, scandalous, or transgressive elements to attract readership and provoke moral commentary. Anti-pattern: restrained or policy-focused reporting that omits sensational detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic clashes of personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict centered on individuals, often exaggerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalize stories around vivid personalities and magnify clashes to create drama; use caricature and hyperbole. Avoid systemic or institutional explanations that dilute personal drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outsiders vs. insiders themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurring theme distinguishing insiders (the community) from outsiders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct narratives that align readers with an 'inside' group and oppose perceived outsiders to reinforce community boundaries. Use language and story selection to mark insiders as deserving and outsiders as threatening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women as a thematic focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent thematic focus on women, often objectified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories and images disproportionately foreground women, sometimes in objectifying ways; this may serve voyeuristic or moralizing functions. Be alert to gendered framing and the ethical implications of objectification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy use of famous names and celebrity-focused content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage celebrity personalities and scandals to drive attention and emotional investment; name recognition is a primary attention hook. Contrast with broadsheet emphasis on institutional actors and policy-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nostalgia
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to the British past to evoke sentiment and identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke nostalgic images, language, and references to create a sense of shared heritage and cultural continuity among readers. Use selective memory to idealize past social forms or national identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactionary moralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Moralizing rhetoric often framed in working-class terms and resistant to progressive change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a moral tone that defends 'common-sense' values and castigates perceived moral decline; this can mobilize readers' conservative sentiments. Anti-pattern: progressive or reformist framings that challenge traditional morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagined community of readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial practices that construct and address an imagined collective readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select stories, tone, and address to speak to a cohesive readership identity—shared values, resentments, and humor—thereby reinforcing community bonds. Evaluate how language and story choices signal inclusion/exclusion of readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabloid weighting of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabloids prioritize human emotion, transgression, celebrity, moral judgment, and vivid drama when judging what is newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing tabloid content, emphasize emotional resonance, scandal, personal stories, moral framing, and dramatic presentation over institutional significance. Use vividness and readability as key selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadsheet weighting of newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadsheets prioritize institutional importance, policy implications, complexity, and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast criterion: broadsheets value stories for their relevance to institutions, policy consequence, and analytical depth. This is a useful comparator when classifying or assessing differences between tabloid and broadsheet treatment of events.
